In collaboration with De Appel, on 21 May between 18:30—20:30 CEST, we present the event "Culture is — arts, imagination, and the planetary now", exploring culture as an urgent necessity that offers relational language, radical imagination, and care.

Cover image courtesy of 2025 Building Beyond Fellow Ìfẹ́olúwa Ọ̀ṣúnkọ̀yà.

In this conversation, Teesa Bahana (Director of 32° East, a not-for-profit contemporary art space in Uganda, currently on study leave) and Ola Hassanain (artist and architect) will explore our time of ecological collapse, political fragmentation, and growing inequality, in which culture is not a luxury—it is a necessity. Yet around the world, artists and cultural spaces are under threat: defunded, censored, co-opted, or erased entirely. In this moment of planetary crisis, the arts provide a language of relation, a tool for radical imagination, and a practice of care that transcends borders.

What forms of solidarity, policy, and institutional rethinking are needed to sustain artistic communities across geographies? What does it mean to cultivate a planetary consciousness rooted in justice and imagination?

Culture shapes how we live, how we move through the world, and how we relate to the land and to each other. As civic and artistic freedoms shrink under the weight of nationalism, austerity, and extractive systems, we must ask not only how to defend cultural space, but how to expand it.

Featured speakers

Teesa
Bahana

Ola
Hassanain

Building Beyond Senior Fellow

This conversation is part of Exchanges, the Fund’s platform for creative cross-pollination that connects our international network with Amsterdam’s cultural landscape while building long-lasting relationships across the city’s diverse artistic scenes. Exchanges is made possible through the generous support from the City of Amsterdam.

items.content_html:
How can art and culture empower us to fight the climate emergency, build the cities of tomorrow and rewrite dominant narratives? We are proud to introduce 37 new Fellows whose work critically engages with these questions.

Cover: "50 Years of Forgetting" by Moving Narratives Fellow Mai Huyền Chi.

The Fellows Award facilitates mid-career artists in amplifying socially engaged practices while building meaningful connections within a global network of like-minded creatives. Each Fellow receives €10.000 to advance their work, along with access to opportunities to expand their work’s impact.

Learn more about their inspiring work below!

Moving Narratives

9 Fellows across disciplines—from artistic research, film and performance to visual and video art—respond to histories, racial justice, and the climate crisis, challenging the boundaries between art, politics, and history.

CAREC

9 Fellows critically addressing the connection between the climate justice and the social, racial, and environmental issues through media studies, curatorial practice, visual arts, filmmaking, sound art, and design.

Building Beyond

9 Fellows representing 6 African countries reimagining the future of their homelands through architecture, urbanism, digital design, research, and performance, with a shared focus on the circular economy, collective history, and community.

ADPP

10 Fellows exploring themes of displacement and migration, personal and collective trauma, memory and identity, and the intimate, often overlooked realities of everyday life.

As these four new cohorts unfold, the Fellows’ practices invite us to reconsider how art can respond to and reshape the urgencies of our time. Rooted in diverse contexts yet connected through shared concerns, their work exemplifies culture as a fundamental force for change.

items.content_html:
In 2025, we celebrated the determination, resilience, and creative courage of our network of changemakers in times when cultural and civic freedoms are facing pressures. These conditions reaffirmed our commitment to stand alongside those working to protect and sustain spaces for free cultural expression.

Cover: courtesy of Gabriel Pinto, 2024 Seed Awardee.

“Our work is rooted in people and their stories: in the connections they build, the risks they take, and the possibilities they open for others. None of this is self-evident. It is sustained through investment, trust, solidarity, and long-term commitment. Culture is a life-changing force — and one that demands our collective care and preservation.”

— Hendrikje Crebolder, Interim Director of Prince Claus Fund

Supporting artists and changemakers in contexts where culture is under pressure means continuing to invest in the conditions that allow their work to endure—through trust-based funding, recognition, and meaningful connections. In doing so, we contribute to maintaining safe cultural spaces where freedom of expression and independent thinking can take shape, and where diverse voices can be shared.

Explore the impact stories of 2025

Last year, we launched our pilot Urgency Programme, supported by the Postcode Lottery, to provide urgent assistance to our global network of Awardees facing oppression, war, natural disasters, and unforeseen circumstances. In its first phase, the programme were able to support 44 artists across 32 countries, ensuring them to continue their vital work in times of crisis.

Throughout the year, our Fellows Awards Lab Weeks continued to play an important role in fostering connections and knowledge exchange. The strength of community amplifies the value of diverse perspectives, making artistic practices more meaningful and socially impactful.

In addition to Nepal, Indonesia, and Mozambique, Lab Week was also held in Amsterdam and Rotterdam, the Netherlands, to strengthen connections between our Fellows and Dutch artists, organisations, and local audiences. This collaboration promotes mutual learning, sparks innovation, and creates opportunities for cross-cultural dialogue. 

“Just the privilege to be able to create freely, as true as it can be to my vision and how I would like to express myself without worrying about external factors on my livelihood.”

— Htet Aung Lwyn, Seed Awardee (Myanmar & Thailand)

A key moment in 2025 was Exchanges, a programme facilitated with the generous support from the City of Amsterdam. We collaborated with Eye Filmmuseum and the Netherlands Film Academy and brought together the diverse voices of Prince Claus Awardees from the Global South and the city’s cultural communities, Exchanges brought different practices and perspectives into dialogue. It opened up new ways of thinking for local artists, cultural workers, and audiences, while strengthening a sense of international solidarity within the city’s cultural fabric.

Read about these and many other stories in the 2025 Annual Report!

items.content_html:
2026 marks 30 years since the establishment of the Prince Claus Fund—three decades of standing alongside artists and cultural practitioners working where culture and freedom of expression are under pressure.

Cover image courtesy of 2024 Seed Awardee Gabriel Pinto.

We are proud to kick off our anniversary celebrations at TEFAF Maastricht 2026 between 14-19 March with the presentation of powerful work by Prince Claus Award Recipient Ibrahim Mahama, one of the most influential artists of his generation.

If you happen to be at TEFAF Maastricht 2026, visit our booth and to encounter Mahama’s new work firsthand: titled "Sénégal Fast Food", it continues the artist's long-standing engagement with material histories, labour, and processes of extraction and abandonment. Central to the work is the extension of the life of objects once embedded in systems of commodity production.

Mahama’s work invites us to reinterpret social and economic histories beyond conventional boundaries, reflecting the kind of free artistic expression the Fund strives to safeguard: one that centres autonomy, experimentation, and diverse voices.

Alongside this presentation, we will also host a curated library featuring landmark publications by Irma Boom, a renown visionary in book design whose collaboration with the Fund goes back to our founding days.

Marking our 30-year anniversary, we look ahead—continuing to invest in future talent and artists at crucial stages in their careers, those who will shape the cultural landscape of our time. We support artists long before the art market or global audiences take notice, offering early recognition and sustained encouragement when it matters most.

Our commitment is grounded in trust and long-term relationships with our community, from emerging talents finding their voice to established creators whose work resonates across borders and beyond art market trends. By championing artistic freedom, collective imagination, and exchange, the Fund connects you to the vibrant cultural pulse of its global community.

Because culture is a force. For open and free societies.  

About Ibrahim Mahama

Ibrahim Mahama (b. 1987, Tamale, Ghana), 2020 Prince Claus Fund Awardee and International Advisory Board member, embodies the changemakers the Fund supports. Based between Accra and Tamale, his practice uses jute sacks, wood, paper, and everyday objects to reveal hidden narratives of labour, migration, and global exchange.

Founder of the Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art, Red Clay, and Nkrumah Volini, Mahama has shaped Ghana’s contemporary art scene. Named ArtReview’s most influential artist in 2025, his work has been shown internationally and is held in major collections. His awards include the Sam Gilliam Award (2024) and the Art Basel Gold Award (2025), and the Republic of Ghana granted him a diplomatic passport in recognition of his cultural impact.

About Irma Boom

Irma Boom is a bookmaker based in Amsterdam and the designer of more than 500 books, known for her radical, experimental approach that challenges the conventions of the book as both object and medium. Since 1992, she has served as Senior Critic at Yale University and lectures internationally. Boom’s work is held in major collections, including MoMA New York, the Art Institute of Chicago, the Vatican Library, and Centre Pompidou, with her complete oeuvre preserved at the University of Amsterdam. She has received the Gutenberg Prize, the Johannes Vermeer Award, and an honorary doctorate from the Royal College of Art, London.

A longstanding partner of the Prince Claus Fund, Boom has shaped the Fund’s visual identity through her book designs and the creation of its iconic logo.

We wish to thank TEFAF, Irma Boom, Stabilo International, and Maison Ruinart for their partnership making the Fund’s presence at TEFAF possible.

items.content_html:
The Prince Claus Fund is proud to announce that we received €1.5 million contribution from the Dutch Postcode Lottery to establish the Urgency Programme.

With this capital, we can now establish the Urgency Programme which will provide urgent assistance to artists from the global Prince Claus Fund network facing oppression, war, and natural disasters. The Urgency Programme will ensure that artists can continue their vital work under even the most challenging circumstances.

The Prince Claus Fund Executive Director, Marcus Desando highlights the impact that the new Fund will have on artists, stating that:

"Beyond immediate financial aid, the Fund will also invest in long-term solutions. We will be developing a toolkit to share knowledge, foster an international support network, and work to enhance the resilience of artists and their communities." 

Artists play a crucial role in defending freedom, justice, and equality. In times of crisis, their creative expression becomes a powerful tool against oppression and injustice. Yet, traditional humanitarian aid often overlooks the importance of protecting artistic freedom. The Urgency Programme addresses this gap by offering rapid financial support and protection to the Prince Claus Fund Awardees facing risks, helping them to sustain their practice and resilience.

This initiative will ensure that, even in times of crisis, artists can continue to inspire, illuminate complex realities, and advocate for a more just and inclusive world.

Jonne Arnoldussen, Managing Director of the Dutch Postcode Lottery, emphasizes the Fund’s significance, asserting that:

"Art and culture are essential to the well-being of communities, especially in times of crisis. We are proud that, thanks to our participants, we can support the Prince Claus Fund in its commitment to artists facing oppression, war, and natural disasters. The Urgency Programme will be a crucial lifeline for preserving cultural expression worldwide."

The support of the Postcode Lottery for the past 25 years has been essential for the successful continuation of the Prince Claus Fund work, and we are excited to have the longstanding partnership exist to this day. With the indispensable support of the Postcode Lottery, the Prince Claus Fund is committed to safeguarding artistic freedom and strengthening creative resilience where it is needed most.

More information about the programme will be announced in the coming months.

items.content_html:
The Prince Claus Fund is deeply concerned for the safety of our partners in Palestine and the Arab region. Currently, our Arab Documentary Photography Programme. Fellows Samar Abu Elouf and Sameh Rahmi, both based in Gaza, are in grave danger of documenting and sharing the stories of the people on the ground.

Cover Image © Sameh Rahmi/ Photojournalist/ Gaza Strip.

We condemn and mourn the many civilian Palestine, Israeli, and Lebanese lives lost, and, together with institutional funders, individual donors, and philanthropy professionals globally, we are calling for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and safe, unimpeded passage of humanitarian aid. Please read the full statement here.

The Prince Claus Fund has long been committed to supporting artists and cultural practitioners in Palestine and the Arab region - from awarding some of the most prolific and inspiring Palestinian artists, such as poet Mahmoud Darwish to developing a longstanding Arab Documentary Photography Programme, together with Arab Funds For Art and Culture and Magnum Foundation. Driven by our vision of a world where free and valued cultural expression creates an equitable, peaceful, sustainable and inclusive future, we will continue supporting and amplifying their voices.

This is a call for all international funders to join the statement and call for adherence to international humanitarian and human rights. Beyond providing urgent humanitarian aid, the international community needs to commit to supporting Palestinian civil society in the long-term.
